scenes.say: A build broke somewhere in the last hundred commits, and you don't know which. By the end, you'll find the culprit in seven tries, then tell that hunt as a story that lands the offer.
Today you will do three things. Find the bad commit by halving history. Merge or rebase a branch, and fix a conflict. And tell your bug story in ninety seconds.
lines: Find the bad commit by halving history
Merge or rebase, and fix a conflict
Tell a bug story in 90 seconds

scenes.title: Which commit broke the build?
scenes.statement: The last release worked and today's build fails. A hundred commits sit between. Find the first bad one.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. Today's build fails, and the last release worked. For example, a hundred commits between, first good, last bad. We want the culprit, in seven tests.

scenes.head: A detective, not a gambler
scenes.say: Interviewers test your method, not your luck. A detective doesn't guess. First, reproduce: make it fail on demand. Second, minimize: shrink the failing input. Third, bisect: halve the history. Fourth, fix it, and add a test.

scenes.head: Hunting through 100 commits
scenes.say: This chart counts tests. Commit one worked, commit one hundred broke. Checking one by one could take ninety eight tests. Halving the range takes seven.

scenes.head: Bisect: 8 commits, 3 tests
scenes.say: Eight commits. Commit one worked, commit eight is broken. Test the middle one, c four. Passes, so the bug is later. Test c six. Fails, so the culprit is c five or c six. Test c five. Fails again, so c five broke it. Three tests for eight commits.
Your turn. Now a thousand commits, with only the first and last known. In the worst case, how many tests does bisect need? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 1,000 commits, bug somewhere. Worst-case bisect tests?

scenes.head: Let git do the halving
scenes.say: Ten, because two to the tenth is one thousand twenty four. For our hundred, seven halvings are enough. Tell git the current commit is bad, and the commit ninety nine back is good. Bisect run feeds it a test script. Exit zero means good. This run took seven tests, and names the culprit.

panels.code:
git bisect start HEAD HEAD~99 > /dev/null
git bisect run ./test.sh | grep -c running
git log -1 --format=%s refs/bisect/bad
git bisect reset 2>/dev/null

setup.run.sh:
git init -q -b main
git config user.email a@b.c
git config user.name t
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  if [ $i -ge 64 ]; then echo bad > state.txt; else echo ok > state.txt; fi
  echo $i > n.txt
  git add -A
  if [ $i = 64 ]; then m="order id from seconds"; else m="c$i"; fi
  git commit -qm "$m"
done
printf '#!/bin/sh\ngrep -q ok state.txt\n' > test.sh
chmod +x test.sh

scenes.title: Make a bug show itself
scenes.statement: A job fails on a big file, and a test fails now and then. Make each fail on demand, then shrink it.

example.output: a tiny repro that fails every run

scenes.say: Here's the problem. A job and a test fail, and they're hard to catch. For example, a ten thousand row file. We want a tiny repro that fails every run.

scenes.head: Shrink the input until it stops failing
scenes.say: A job fails on a file with ten thousand rows. Don't read them all. Keep the first five thousand: still fails. The first three: passes. The first four: fails. So row four is the culprit, and you hold a tiny repro that becomes your regression test, a test that fails if the bug ever returns.

panels.code:
rows = ["ok"] * 10000
rows[3] = ""
def fails(r):
    return "" in r
print(fails(rows[:5000]), fails(rows[:3]), fails(rows[:4]))

scenes.head: A flaky test: ids from the clock
scenes.say: Now a flaky test. Orders get an id from the clock, in whole seconds. The test passes only when the clock ticks between two orders. Don't wait for luck. Pass the time in, and it fails every run.

panels.code:
orders = {}
def create(now):
    orders[int(now)] = "paid"
create(100.2)
create(100.9)
create(101.1)
print(len(orders))

scenes.say: Three orders arrive at one hundred point two, one hundred point nine, and one hundred one point one. How many orders does the program store? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: After the three `create` calls, what does `len(orders)` print?

scenes.head: Two ids, not three
scenes.say: Two. The first two orders both get id one hundred, so the second overwrites the first. The third gets one oh one. Three orders went in, and the program kept two.

scenes.head: Fix it, then pin it with a test
scenes.say: The fix: stop using the clock as the identity. A counter gives every order its own id. Now three orders go in, every run, on every machine. Add a regression test.

panels.code:
import itertools
ids = itertools.count(1)
orders = {}
def create(now):
    orders[next(ids)] = "paid"
create(100.2)
create(100.9)
create(101.1)
print(len(orders))

scenes.head: Follow-ups on debugging
scenes.say: Follow ups. Can't reproduce it? Add logging, capture the real input. What does bisect need? A good commit and an automatic test. A flaky test? Fix it first, because bisect needs the same verdict each time. Not a commit at all? Check config, data, dependencies. Mistake: changing code before you can reproduce.
rows: Add logging, capture the real input
A good commit + an automatic test
Fix it first: same verdict every run

scenes.title: Combine my branch with main
scenes.statement: Main moved on while you worked. Bring your two commits and the new ones together, readably.

example.input: main: M1 M2 M3; feature: F1 F2
example.output: one history with all five commits

scenes.say: Here's the problem. Main moved on while you worked. For example, main has three commits, yours has two. We want one history with all five.

scenes.head: Your branch and main
scenes.say: Think of a shared recipe book. On Monday you photocopy it: that's M one. Meanwhile others add M two and M three to the book. You write two pages of your own, F one and F two. Each commit points back to its parent. Now your pages must go into the book.

scenes.head: Merge: one commit, two parents
scenes.say: Merge adds one new commit with two parents: the tip of main and the tip of your branch. Nothing old is touched. History shows the work really happened in parallel. The cost: extra merge commits, and a graph that can tangle.

scenes.head: One conflict, resolved
scenes.say: Both sides changed one line, so git stops and asks. Merging your branch into main, the top half is main's version. The bottom half is yours. Edit the file to the final result, here sixty, and delete the three marker lines. Then git add the file and commit.

output.text:
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.py
Automatic merge failed

scenes.say: Your turn. Rebase is the other way to combine: it copies your commits onto the tip of main. Same branch, rebased onto M three. How many new commits does git create? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Rebase F1, F2 onto M3. New commits created?

scenes.head: Rebase: replay on top
scenes.say: Two. Rebase replays each of your commits as a copy on top of M three: F one prime and F two prime. The result is a straight line. But the copies have new hashes, and the old F one and F two are abandoned. You rewrote history, so never rebase commits other people already have.

scenes.head: Follow-ups on merge and rebase
scenes.say: Follow ups. Which do you use? Rebase mine, merge shared branches. Rebase went badly? Rebase abort puts you back. Pushing after a rebase? Force with lease, only on my own branch. Mistake: rebasing a branch others already pulled.
rows: Rebase my own branch; merge shared ones
Rebasing a branch others already pulled

scenes.title: Tell me about a hard bug
scenes.statement: The interviewer says: tell me about a hard bug you fixed. You get about ninety seconds.

example.input: the bug hunt: 100 commits, found in 7
example.output: a story with a result they remember

scenes.say: Here's the problem. The interviewer says, tell me about a hard bug you fixed. For example, our bisect hunt, a hundred commits, found in seven. We want a story with a result they remember.

scenes.head: S.T.A.R. for the bisect hunt
scenes.say: Tell it with S T A R, using your own real story. Mine's made up. Situation: the checkout test failed after a hundred commits. Task: find the cause before release. Action: I froze the clock, then bisected in seven runs. Result: a counter fix, plus a test.

scenes.head: Where the 90 seconds go
scenes.say: This chart splits the ninety seconds. Situation, about fifteen. Task, ten. Action, forty five, because that's where you show how you think. Result, twenty, ending on a number.
Your turn. Four ways to say the action part. Which one lands the offer? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Which Action line lands the offer?

scenes.head: Weak line, strong line
scenes.say: The third one. It names the method and a count. Weak lines say we, and stay vague. Name the real cause: ids from whole seconds. End on a count: seven runs, plus a test.
rows: I froze the clock, then bisected
I wrote the fix and the test
Root cause: ids from whole seconds

scenes.head: A second story shape
scenes.say: A second shape. Symptom: a web app showed a wrong score, only sometimes. Reproduce: send requests in parallel. Root cause: both requests read the same score, and one write overwrote the other. Fix: one atomic update. Prevent: a concurrency test.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: A bug that only happens sometimes? Reproduce, shrink, bisect, fix, add a test. Can't reproduce it? Add logging. What does bisect need? A good commit and an automatic test. Mistake: changing code first.
rows: Add logging, capture the real input

scenes.say: Merge versus rebase? Merge: a commit with two parents. Rebase: replay, new hashes. Conflicts? Edit, delete markers, add, continue. Which one? Rebase mine, merge shared, then force with lease.
lines: Merge: two parents. Rebase: replay, new hashes.
Conflict: edit, delete markers, add, continue.
Rebase mine, merge shared. Then force-with-lease.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: A hard bug you fixed? Situation, task, action, result, about ninety seconds. Do differently? Add monitoring earlier. How did you know? A measurement and a test. Mistake: we, long background, no result.
rows: STAR, ~90 seconds, name the root cause
A before and after number, plus a test

scenes.head: Practice this week
scenes.say: Three exercises. Build a repo with a hundred commits and a planted bug, and bisect it. Cause a conflict, and resolve it by merge, then by rebase. And tell your own bug in S T A R, timed at ninety seconds.
rows: Bisect a 100-commit repo with a planted bug
Resolve one conflict by merge, then by rebase
Tell one real bug in STAR form, timed

scenes.say: So say this. Reproduce, shrink, bisect: a hundred commits, seven tests. Merge keeps history, rebase straightens it, never on shared branches. In S T A R, name the cause, say I, end on a result.
lines: Merge keeps history. Rebase rewrites it, never shared.
STAR: real root cause, say I, end on a result.
